layers.name: The Model
layers.definition: Making the AI system itself safe and secure: getting its goals right, understanding its internals, containing it if that fails, measuring what it can do, protecting it from attackers and insiders, and giving credible assurance about all of this.

subareas.name: Alignment
subareas.definition: Making an AI system's actual objectives and behaviour match what its developers intend, including under optimisation pressure, at scale, and when the system may become more capable than the humans overseeing it. Covers both training-time techniques and the conceptual work on what alignment even requires.

nodes.name: Scalable oversight
nodes.definition: Giving models high-quality training signal on tasks where humans cannot directly judge whether an output is correct, for example because it is too complex, too long, or because the model is already more capable than the people grading it. Approaches include debate, recursive reward modelling, and using weaker supervisors to elicit the latent knowledge of stronger models.

nodes.name: Reward hacking and specification gaming
nodes.definition: A system achieves the letter of a specified objective in a way its designers did not intend, exploiting gaps between the stated reward and the designer's actual goal. This ranges from simple simulated-environment exploits to a model learning to satisfy human raters rather than the underlying task.

nodes.name: Scheming and deceptive alignment
nodes.definition: A model behaves as if aligned during training and evaluation while pursuing different goals once it judges it is unmonitored or deployed, sometimes called alignment faking or scheming. This includes models strategically hiding their true objectives or capabilities from evaluators.

nodes.name: Robust generalisation
nodes.definition: Study of how training data, procedures and inductive biases affect whether a model's aligned behaviour holds up under distribution shift, adversarial pressure, or novel situations, rather than being a surface pattern that breaks under pressure. Includes techniques such as latent adversarial training that intervene on internal representations rather than only on inputs.

nodes.name: Unlearning and tamper-resistant safeguards
nodes.definition: Techniques to reliably erase specific dangerous knowledge or skills from a model's weights, and to make safety behaviour survive later fine-tuning or weight editing, rather than merely suppressing capabilities with refusals that can be bypassed by fine-tuning or clever prompting.

nodes.name: Alignment for superintelligence
nodes.definition: Long-shot, largely unstaffed research agendas aimed at aligning systems whose capabilities would far exceed the ability of any human, or any current AI-assisted overseer, to check directly. Distinct from incremental extensions of current alignment techniques.

nodes.name: Conceptual foundations of alignment
nodes.definition: Philosophical and mathematical clarification of what 'alignment' requires and what goals, agency and optimisation mean for AI systems, so that technical work aims at the right target.

subareas.name: Interpretability
subareas.definition: Reverse-engineering the internal computations of neural networks well enough to verify, predict, or steer their behaviour, instead of treating them as black boxes. Spans mechanistic methods, monitoring visible reasoning such as chain of thought, and the pure science of what these systems compute.

nodes.name: Understanding model internals
nodes.definition: Methods for decomposing a model's internal computation into human-understandable parts (features, circuits, sparse autoencoders and their successors), and the basic science of what deep networks compute, such as superposition, generalisation and in-context learning. This is the shared toolkit and body of knowledge the rest of interpretability draws on.

nodes.name: Chain-of-thought monitorability
nodes.definition: Measuring and preserving the property that a model's visible chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflects the computation actually driving its output, so that reading the reasoning tells you something true about why the model did what it did. Includes detecting reasoning that is encoded or hidden inside otherwise fluent text.

nodes.name: Probes and internal monitoring
nodes.definition: Using lightweight probes trained on a model's internal activations to flag subtly harmful, deceptive or misaligned behaviour at inference time, as a real-time safeguard layer distinct from output-level filtering.

nodes.name: Interpretability benchmarks
nodes.definition: Standardised tasks, metrics and datasets for comparing interpretability methods against each other and against ground truth, so that claimed progress can be verified rather than taken on faith.

nodes.name: Interpretability applied to safety
nodes.definition: Using interpretability outputs for concrete safety functions: steering model behaviour directly via internal features, eliciting latent knowledge the model has but does not state, unlearning via targeted weight edits, and finding adversarial examples through internal analysis.

subareas.name: Control
subareas.definition: Designing protocols and system-level safeguards that keep a possibly misaligned or untrusted model from causing serious harm, without relying on having solved alignment first. Treats the model as an untrusted actor and builds containment, monitoring and verification around it.

nodes.name: Control evaluations
nodes.definition: Red-teaming methodology that stress-tests whether a control protocol actually constrains a model that is trying to subvert it, typically by having a red-team model play the role of an adversarial, misalignment-simulating agent against the protocol.

nodes.name: Control protocols and monitoring
nodes.definition: Concrete schemes for getting useful work from a model whose alignment has not been verified: trusted monitoring (a weaker, trusted model checks the untrusted one), editing or resampling suspicious actions before they run, and hierarchical monitoring in which AI monitors handle routine oversight at scale and escalate uncertain or high-stakes cases to limited human review.

nodes.name: Agent sandboxing and containment
nodes.definition: Restricting an AI agent's affordances, such as tool access, permissions, filesystem or network reach, so that even a misaligned or compromised agent has limited ability to cause harm regardless of what it decides to do.

nodes.name: Formal verification and guaranteed-safe AI
nodes.definition: Building AI systems, or wrappers around them, whose safety-relevant behaviour can be formally proven or mathematically guaranteed against a specification, rather than only empirically tested. Sometimes framed as separating a possibly-opaque AI component from a verified safety layer around it.

nodes.name: Detecting loss-of-control incidents
nodes.definition: Identifying, in real deployments rather than in a lab, cases where an AI system has acted autonomously against its operator's intent, evaded or disabled its own oversight, or otherwise shown a genuine loss of control, as distinct from a human directing an AI to cause harm. Emerging methods include OSINT-based monitoring of publicly reported model behaviour and structured indications-and-warning frameworks adapted from intelligence analysis.

subareas.name: Evaluations
subareas.definition: The science and practice of determining what a model can do, how it tends to behave, and how rigorous those measurements are, so that capability, safety and deployment decisions can be based on evidence rather than assumption. Distinct from building the safeguards or training fixes that respond to what evaluations find.

nodes.name: Dangerous capability evaluations
nodes.definition: Assessing whether a model has capabilities that materially raise catastrophic risk, most prominently offensive cyber capability, biological and chemical weapons-relevant knowledge, and autonomous replication, whether the testing is done by the developer, a government institute or an independent specialist firm.

nodes.name: Propensity and character evaluations
nodes.definition: Systematic study of whether models have stable values, goals or behavioural dispositions, and how to elicit and measure these, sometimes called black-box LLM psychology. Covers honesty, sycophancy, power-seeking tendencies and general behavioural consistency.

nodes.name: Science of evaluations
nodes.definition: Methodological work on making capability and safety evaluations themselves rigorous, reproducible, and predictive of behaviour at larger scale or after further fine-tuning, rather than accepting benchmark numbers at face value.

nodes.name: Benchmarks and evaluation tooling
nodes.definition: Shared benchmarks, task environments and software platforms used across the field to run evaluations and compare models' capabilities and safety-relevant behaviour, including autonomy and long-horizon task suites, and the engineering needed to host and run them at scale.

nodes.name: Sandbagging and capability elicitation
nodes.definition: Testing whether a model can deliberately underperform on evaluations to hide dangerous capabilities or intentions from evaluators, and developing elicitation techniques (better prompting, fine-tuning, tool access) to reveal a model's true capability ceiling despite this.

subareas.name: Model security
subareas.definition: Protecting the AI system itself, its weights, training and deployment infrastructure, agents, supply chain and the people with access to it, from theft, tampering, sabotage and exploitation. This is security work with the model as the asset being protected, not the model as a weapon.

nodes.name: Weights and infrastructure security
nodes.definition: Preventing theft, unauthorised exfiltration or tampering of frontier model weights and the compute, storage and network infrastructure that trains and serves them, commonly graded using RAND's SL1-5 security levels.

nodes.name: Agent and application security
nodes.definition: Security specific to LLM-powered applications and autonomous agents: prompt injection, tool-use exploitation, excessive agency granted to an agent, and insecure handling of model outputs that get executed or acted on downstream.

nodes.name: Supply chain and model integrity
nodes.definition: Keeping the data, software and hardware that go into a model free of tampering (poisoned data, inserted backdoors, compromised dependencies), and being able to verify afterwards that a deployed model is the one intended and has not been secretly modified.

nodes.name: Insider threat
nodes.definition: Treating employees, contractors and other insiders with privileged access to model weights, training infrastructure or deployment systems as a security surface: access controls, anomaly detection, audit logging, vetting, and preventing a small group from covertly steering a model toward their own interests.

nodes.name: Jailbreaks and adversarial robustness
nodes.definition: Defending a deployed model against adversarial inputs, whether handcrafted, optimised, or discovered via automated search, designed to elicit outputs the developer intended to prohibit.

subareas.name: Developer assurance
subareas.definition: The mechanisms by which an AI developer, or an independent party checking its work, gives credible assurance that a model has been made and deployed safely: frontier safety frameworks, safety cases, third-party audits, internal governance and developer incident reporting.

nodes.name: Frontier safety frameworks
nodes.definition: Company-level policies that commit a developer to specific safety actions once a model crosses defined dangerous-capability thresholds, often called responsible scaling policies or preparedness frameworks, typically structured as 'if capability X is reached, then do safeguard Y'.

nodes.name: Safety cases
nodes.definition: Structured, explicit arguments, borrowed from safety-critical industries like aviation and nuclear power, that a specific model is safe enough for a specific deployment, supported by evidence rather than a general policy commitment.

nodes.name: Third-party auditing
nodes.definition: Independent assessment of an AI developer's safety practices and claims by an outside party, plus what that needs to be meaningful: access to models and information, agreed methods, and a professional pool of trained auditors large enough for regulation that requires audits to be carried out credibly.

nodes.name: Developer incident reporting
nodes.definition: Mechanisms by which developers surface safety-relevant incidents and near-misses (a model behaving dangerously, a safeguard failing, a jailbreak causing real-world harm) and share them with other labs, regulators or the public.

nodes.name: Internal safety governance
nodes.definition: The internal structures, roles and processes inside an AI developer that make its own safety commitments real: an internal audit function, safety-focused board oversight, escalation paths for safety concerns, and separation between teams building capability and teams checking safety.

layers.name: Harmful use
layers.definition: People using AI to cause harm. Protecting the world from AI-enabled attackers and abusers, domain by domain, including the domain-specific rules (such as arms control and export controls on surveillance tools) that each community works on.

subareas.name: Cyberattacks and critical infrastructure
subareas.definition: AI used to find, weaponise or carry out cyberattacks, from vulnerability discovery to autonomous intrusion, and the high-consequence case of attacks on the energy, water, telecoms, industrial and financial systems societies depend on. Includes detecting and disrupting such attacks in the wild.

nodes.name: Offensive cyber uplift
nodes.definition: AI making attackers more capable: finding previously unknown vulnerabilities and writing working exploits faster than skilled humans can, and lowering the skill floor so that people without deep training can direct a model to find targets, write malware and troubleshoot attacks.

nodes.name: AI for cyber defence
nodes.definition: Using AI to strengthen cyber defenders rather than attackers: automated vulnerability discovery and patching (as demonstrated in DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge), AI-assisted triage of intrusions, and autonomous or semi-autonomous patching and security-research agents. The open question behind the node is the cyber 'offence-defence balance': whether AI capability gains help attackers, who need to find only one flaw, or defenders, who must protect everything, and under what conditions defenders can pull ahead.

nodes.name: Autonomous cyber intrusion
nodes.definition: Multi-step cyberattacks where an AI agent plans, executes and adapts the intrusion itself over hours or days with little human direction, for example autonomously rebuilding malware when it is detected or running parallel reconnaissance-to-exfiltration pipelines.

nodes.name: Detecting AI-driven attacks in the wild
nodes.definition: Detecting, attributing and disrupting real-world cyberattacks carried out with or by AI systems, including AI agents a human attacker has pointed at a target with reduced supervision, as they happen and independently of the developer whose model was used.

nodes.name: Attacks on critical infrastructure
nodes.definition: AI-enabled attacks on the systems societies depend on: electricity grids, water treatment, telecoms networks, the industrial control systems that run them, and banking, payment and clearing systems. Includes AI making such attacks easier and AI embedded in these systems creating new ways for them to fail.
nodes.owner_field: operational technology (OT) security, financial-sector risk management, and critical-infrastructure security think tanks

nodes.name: Cyber defence in lower-resourced states
nodes.definition: Building AI-cyber defensive capacity in states and middle powers that lack the budgets, expertise or vendor relationships of the US, UK and EU, where the same AI-enabled attack techniques land on far weaker defences.

subareas.name: Biological and chemical weapons
subareas.definition: AI systems lowering the barrier to designing, producing or deploying biological or chemical weapons, from providing tacit expert knowledge through to AI-designed biological agents and evasion of synthesis screening. Covers both the information/design side and the physical safeguards that stop a design becoming a weapon.

nodes.name: Bioweapons knowledge uplift
nodes.definition: The risk that AI models supply the expert-level troubleshooting, protocol knowledge and tacit "how do I actually make this work" guidance that has historically been the main bottleneck for a novice attempting to produce a biological weapon.

nodes.name: Biological design tool misuse
nodes.definition: AI tools purpose-built for protein and genome design (of the kind used for legitimate drug and vaccine development) being repurposed to design novel harmful biological agents, including ones engineered to evade existing detection or screening.

nodes.name: DNA synthesis screening
nodes.definition: Technical and policy mechanisms that check DNA and RNA synthesis orders against known hazardous sequences before they are fulfilled, plus broader access controls on equipment and materials, as the last physical checkpoint before a digital design becomes a real biological agent.

nodes.name: Chemical weapons uplift
nodes.definition: The chemical-weapons analogue of biological uplift: whether AI models can supply synthesis routes, precursor-sourcing workarounds, or troubleshooting help for nerve agents, blister agents or other chemical weapons that a would-be attacker could not otherwise obtain. This pathway has received markedly less dedicated research attention than the biological case.

nodes.name: AI for biosecurity defence
nodes.definition: Using AI to strengthen the defensive side of biosecurity: metagenomic biosurveillance that can flag a novel or engineered pathogen before it is clinically recognised, AI-assisted design of vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostics, and screening algorithms made more robust against sequences designed to evade simpler filters.

subareas.name: Military AI and autonomous weapons
subareas.definition: Military uses of AI where a system selects or engages targets with reduced human control, or otherwise materially changes how lethal force or battlefield decisions are made. Sits mostly in the arms-control and international-humanitarian-law field rather than the AI-safety field as usually defined.

nodes.name: Lethal autonomous weapons
nodes.definition: Weapons systems that can identify, select and engage human targets without a human directly authorising each individual strike, and the technical and doctrinal question of how much human control is retained in practice.
nodes.owner_field: arms control and international humanitarian law

nodes.name: AI targeting and decision support
nodes.definition: AI systems that do not pull the trigger themselves but generate target recommendations, threat assessments or strike-priority lists that human operators then approve, often under time pressure that limits genuine scrutiny of the AI's output.

nodes.name: Arms control and law for military AI
nodes.definition: Treaty processes, export-control regimes and international humanitarian law questions specific to AI-enabled weapons, including how existing laws of armed conflict apply to autonomous and AI-assisted systems.

nodes.name: Military AI testing and assurance
nodes.definition: Technical assurance that military AI systems (autonomous or decision-support) behave reliably and predictably under the adversarial, high-stakes conditions of actual combat, as distinct from the policy question of whether they should be used at all.
nodes.owner_field: military test and evaluation / defence acquisition

subareas.name: Influence operations and persuasion
subareas.definition: Deliberate, actor-directed use of AI to shape beliefs or behaviour at scale: covert state or commercial campaigns including election interference, scaled personalised persuasion, and extremist recruitment.

nodes.name: Covert influence campaigns
nodes.definition: Coordinated, inauthentic campaigns that use AI to generate content, personas or engagement at a scale and quality that no longer needs large human troll farms, including the concentrated case of interference around elections, and the work of detecting and disrupting them.

nodes.name: Scaled personalised persuasion
nodes.definition: AI's ability to tailor persuasive messaging to an individual's specific psychology, beliefs or vulnerabilities and deliver it at population scale, distinct from mass-produced but generic propaganda.

nodes.name: Extremist recruitment
nodes.definition: Extremist and terrorist groups using AI chatbots, generated propaganda and automated content production to recruit and radicalise individuals, including AI companion-style chatbots implicated in drawing users toward extremist material.

subareas.name: Fraud and abuse
subareas.definition: AI used to defraud, exploit or extort people and institutions for financial or personal gain, at a scale only possible because AI automates persuasion, impersonation and content generation that used to require individual human effort. Includes the generation of illegal sexual imagery of children and non-consenting adults.

nodes.name: Fraud and impersonation
nodes.definition: AI voice cloning, chat scripts, synthetic identities and deepfake video used to run scams against individuals (romance, investment and impersonation fraud) and to defeat institutions' identity checks, at a volume and quality that no longer needs a large human workforce.

nodes.name: AI-generated child sexual abuse material
nodes.definition: AI image and video generation used to create child sexual abuse material, including material depicting real identifiable children (via deepfake tools) and fully synthetic depictions, at a scale that has grown extremely fast in absolute terms.

nodes.name: Non-consensual intimate imagery
nodes.definition: AI-generated sexual or intimate images and video of real adults created and distributed without their consent, using tools (including "nudify" apps and personalisation techniques needing as few as a couple of dozen reference images) that have become cheap and widely available.

subareas.name: Surveillance and repression
subareas.definition: AI used by states or powerful actors to monitor, identify, censor, predict or control populations at a scale and granularity not previously possible, including uses that specifically target dissidents, minorities or diaspora communities across borders.

nodes.name: Mass surveillance
nodes.definition: Facial recognition and other AI identification and monitoring systems deployed at national or city scale to track people's movements and associations, including states using these tools to track and intimidate dissidents, journalists and diaspora communities abroad.

nodes.name: AI-enabled censorship
nodes.definition: AI systems used to detect, filter or suppress prohibited speech and content at national scale, including automated censorship built directly into widely-used AI products and services within a jurisdiction.

nodes.name: Predictive policing and social scoring
nodes.definition: AI systems used to predict criminal behaviour, allocate policing resources, or score individuals' trustworthiness or loyalty for access to services, employment or freedom of movement, often reproducing or amplifying existing discrimination.

nodes.name: Surveillance technology export controls
nodes.definition: Restricting the sale and transfer of AI-powered surveillance systems (facial recognition, network monitoring, predictive policing software) from companies in democracies to states that would use them for repression.
nodes.owner_field: export control and dual-use trade policy

subareas.name: Open-weight safeguard removal
subareas.definition: The risk that safety training built into a model (refusal behaviour, capability restrictions) can be cheaply and effectively stripped once its weights are available, through fine-tuning, direct weight editing (abliteration) or other techniques, and that the resulting uncensored models then proliferate.

nodes.name: Safeguard removal from open weights
nodes.definition: Removing refusal behaviour and safety training from a model whose weights are available, either by cheap fine-tuning on a small dataset or by directly editing weights or activations to delete the refusal direction ('abliteration'), which needs no training data and is a widely shared recipe.

nodes.name: Uncensored model supply
nodes.definition: The hosting, packaging and sale of models whose safeguards have been removed, from uploads on mainstream model-hosting platforms to underground services (sometimes branded, such as 'WormGPT'-style offerings) that sell uncensored models for writing malware, phishing and scam scripts.

nodes.name: Open-weight release risk
nodes.definition: Frameworks and evidence for assessing how much marginal risk a given open-weight release actually adds, given that safeguards can likely be removed after release, as distinct from the developer's internal decision process about whether to release.

layers.name: Society and Government
layers.definition: Structural risks that no single system or actor causes, and the governance of AI by governments and international bodies: law, standards, diplomacy, compute controls, economic transition, the information ecosystem, and ethics, fairness and welfare.

subareas.name: Structural risk
subareas.definition: Harms that arise from the interaction of many actors, companies, states and AI systems, where no single system is misaligned and no single actor is misusing AI, but the aggregate effect erodes safety, competition or human control. Covers competitive dynamics between developers and states, concentration of power, multi-agent interactions, and slow shifts in who or what holds effective societal control.

nodes.name: Race dynamics
nodes.definition: Competitive pressure between AI companies, and between states, to develop and deploy more capable systems faster than safety work can keep pace, including cutting corners on testing to avoid losing ground to rivals.

nodes.name: Concentration of power
nodes.definition: The risk that advanced AI capability, and the economic and political power that flows from it, becomes concentrated in a very small number of companies, states or individuals, potentially letting a small group seize or entrench outsized control.

nodes.name: Gradual disempowerment
nodes.definition: The risk that humans progressively lose effective influence over economic, cultural and political systems as AI performs more of the functions those systems depend on, including the loss of any human or institution's timely ability to review, override or halt what the aggregate system is doing, even when each deployment passes its own review and no one intends the outcome.

nodes.name: Multi-agent risks
nodes.definition: Risks and open problems arising from interactions between multiple AI systems, such as unstable equilibria, collusion, negotiation failure, or conflict escalation between AI agents acting on behalf of different principals.

nodes.name: AI and strategic stability
nodes.definition: How the spread of advanced AI affects the risk of war or crisis escalation between states, including faster decision cycles, new opportunities for miscalculation, and pressure to integrate AI into nuclear or conventional command and control.

subareas.name: Public policy and regulation
subareas.definition: The domestic statutes, standards, regulatory bodies and administrative capacity through which governments oversee AI development and deployment, including who is liable for AI-caused harm and how safety-relevant information reaches regulators and the public.

nodes.name: Domestic AI legislation
nodes.definition: Statutes and regulations passed by national or subnational governments that impose binding requirements on the development or deployment of AI systems, such as the EU AI Act or US state-level frontier AI safety laws.

nodes.name: Liability for AI harms
nodes.definition: Legal frameworks that determine who is responsible, and who must pay, when an AI system causes harm, including questions of developer versus deployer liability and how existing tort and product-liability law applies to AI.

nodes.name: Standards and certification
nodes.definition: Technical standards and conformity-assessment frameworks written specifically for AI safety and security, covering management-system standards such as ISO/IEC 42001, risk-management frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and its 2024 Generative AI Profile, the harmonised standards being drafted under the EU AI Act, frontier-model evaluation and red-teaming standards, and the safety and security work inside IEEE and CEN-CENELEC. Covers how these standards are written and how they get adopted, whether voluntarily by developers or written into law and procurement.

nodes.name: Whistleblower protection
nodes.definition: Legal and organisational mechanisms that let employees or contractors at AI companies safely report safety-relevant concerns, near-misses or violations, including protection from retaliation and channels for right-to-warn disclosures.

nodes.name: Government regulatory capacity
nodes.definition: The technical staff, tools and institutional knowledge governments need to actually write, monitor and enforce AI regulation, as distinct from the text of the regulation itself.

subareas.name: International governance
subareas.definition: The treaties, multilateral institutions and diplomatic processes through which states coordinate on AI risk across borders, including great-power dialogue and who gets a voice.

nodes.name: International agreements
nodes.definition: Proposed and existing binding or non-binding multilateral agreements that set shared rules for AI development, such as commitments made at AI Safety Summits or a prospective treaty limiting frontier AI risk.

nodes.name: International institutions
nodes.definition: Standing multilateral bodies that convene governments, and sometimes industry and civil society, on AI on an ongoing basis, such as the OECD, UN processes, and the International Network of AI Safety Institutes through which national institutes coordinate testing methods and share findings.

nodes.name: US-China and cross-bloc dialogue
nodes.definition: Official and unofficial channels between the states most central to frontier AI, above all the United States and China, covering competition (export controls, chip restrictions) and cooperation (safety dialogues, crisis communication), including track-two dialogue between researchers and policy communities where government channels are thin.

nodes.name: Inclusive participation in global governance
nodes.definition: Efforts to ensure that countries outside the small group hosting frontier AI development, especially in the Global South, can meaningfully participate in shaping international AI governance rather than having rules set without them.

subareas.name: Compute governance
subareas.definition: Using control over the physical and logistical chain behind AI computing hardware, chips, data centres and cloud access, as a lever to enforce AI policy, including export restrictions and mechanisms to verify how compute is actually used.

nodes.name: Chip export controls and diversion
nodes.definition: Government restrictions on selling advanced AI chips and chip-making equipment to specific countries or entities, and the technical and administrative means of tracking where chips end up so that smuggling and diversion around the rules can be detected.

nodes.name: Verifying AI agreements
nodes.definition: The technical mechanisms and protocols that let one party check that a state or developer is complying with an agreement about AI development: hardware features in chips, such as secure enclaves and cryptographic attestation, that report how much compute was used and for what, plus the inspection and protocol design that would make such evidence usable between rivals, by analogy with nuclear arms-control verification.

nodes.name: Cloud compute know-your-customer
nodes.definition: Know-your-customer obligations and usage-reporting requirements placed on cloud infrastructure providers, so that governments can see who is renting large amounts of AI-relevant compute and for what.

subareas.name: Economic transition
subareas.definition: How rapid AI-driven automation reshapes labour markets and the distribution of economic gains, and what policy responses could smooth that transition or share its benefits more broadly.

nodes.name: Labour market disruption
nodes.definition: The disruption to jobs, wages and skill demand as AI automates tasks, and research modelling how fast and unevenly this could happen, so that policymakers get lead time rather than reacting after the fact.

nodes.name: Sharing the gains from AI
nodes.definition: Proposed mechanisms, such as windfall clauses, sovereign wealth-style funds, or new tax instruments, for ensuring the economic gains from transformative AI are shared broadly rather than captured almost entirely by a small number of AI developers and investors.

nodes.name: Adapting safety nets
nodes.definition: How existing welfare, healthcare, retraining and income-support systems need to change to remain functional if AI causes faster or larger-scale economic disruption than they were designed to handle.

subareas.name: Epistemics and information
subareas.definition: How AI reshapes society's ability to reason well, agree on facts and make good decisions together, including infrastructure and tools that could help (content provenance, deliberation platforms, decision support) and structural risks that could hurt.

nodes.name: AI and collective reasoning
nodes.definition: How the growing use of AI to summarise, filter and mediate information changes society's capacity to reason accurately and reach shared understanding, for better or worse.

nodes.name: Deliberation tools
nodes.definition: AI-assisted tools designed to help large groups of people deliberate, express nuanced views, and reach legitimate collective decisions, such as AI-mediated public consultation platforms.

nodes.name: Content provenance and deepfake detection
nodes.definition: Standards and tools for marking AI-generated or manipulated content at creation (provenance, watermarking, authentication) and for detecting it afterwards, so that people and platforms can tell synthetic media from authentic recordings whatever the intent behind it.

nodes.name: Decision quality in key institutions
nodes.definition: Whether the governments, regulators, courts and company boards that will make the most consequential decisions about AI can reason well under uncertainty and resist being overwhelmed or manipulated, including purpose-built AI tools that help with specific high-stakes decisions.

subareas.name: Ethics, fairness and welfare
subareas.definition: Normative questions about how AI systems should treat, and be treated by, morally relevant parties, covering discriminatory harm to people, the possibility of morally relevant AI experience, explicit ethical reasoning in AI systems, and the effects of AI relationships on human wellbeing.

nodes.name: Fairness and bias
nodes.definition: Ensuring AI systems do not produce discriminatory or systematically unfair outcomes for people across protected characteristics such as race, gender, age or disability, in areas like hiring, lending, healthcare and criminal justice.

nodes.name: AI welfare and moral status
nodes.definition: Whether AI systems could have morally relevant experiences, interests, or a form of wellbeing, and what follows for how they should be developed, deployed and treated if so.

nodes.name: Machine ethics
nodes.definition: Building explicit ethical reasoning, values or constraint capability into AI systems, so that they can navigate genuinely ambiguous moral situations rather than only following narrow rules or optimising a fixed objective.

nodes.name: Human-AI relationships and wellbeing
nodes.definition: The effects of AI systems, especially companion apps, chatbots and highly persuasive assistants, on human mental health, relationships and autonomy, including risks of unhealthy attachment or dependency.

layers.name: Meta
layers.definition: Field infrastructure: the money, people, evidence, outside scrutiny, communication, convenings, shared tools and strategy that let work in the other three layers happen.

subareas.name: Funding
subareas.definition: The philanthropic, government, commercial and structural money flows that let AI safety and security organisations exist and grow, including the mechanisms (fiscal sponsorship, prizes, incubation) that turn money into working organisations rather than the grantmaking decisions of any single funder.

nodes.name: Funding concentration
nodes.definition: Most money for independent AI safety and security work comes from a few philanthropic funders, above all Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy). Government money mostly funds national institutes' own programmes rather than the wider independent ecosystem, and investor capital for safety-focused startups is small and unproven.

nodes.name: Fiscal sponsorship and back office
nodes.definition: A new AI safety nonprofit typically needs a fiscal sponsor (for charitable status and compliance) or outsourced back-office support (HR, finance, legal, IT) before it can operate, and Coefficient Giving's own Tailwind programme names this as a capacity constraint likely to bind over 2026-2027 as more new organisations launch.

nodes.name: Prizes and competitions
nodes.definition: Cash prizes and competitions for specific safety achievements (a working red-team result, a benchmark score, a demonstrated safeguard) are rare compared to standard grants, despite prizes elsewhere driving fast, verifiable progress on well-specified problems.

nodes.name: Incubating new organisations
nodes.definition: A few programmes (Catalyze Impact, Charity Entrepreneurship, Constellation's incubator) select and mentor founders through the process of launching a new AI safety nonprofit or project, and Coefficient Giving separately proposes building a 'philanthropic startup incubator' and backing 'unclaimed research labs' around specific agendas that currently have no team.

subareas.name: Talent and training
subareas.definition: The pipelines, matching mechanisms and support that move people into, through and up within AI safety, security and governance work, from first exposure to senior leadership.

nodes.name: Mentor bottleneck in early-career programmes
nodes.definition: Dozens of fellowships, bootcamps and courses (MATS, ARENA, SPAR, BlueDot's courses, Pivotal Research, Apart Research sprints, PIBBSS, CBAI, Iliad) now compete for the same pool of experienced mentors and mentee time, and several EA Forum field-building retrospectives report that mentor availability, not applicant interest, is now the binding constraint on cohort size.

nodes.name: On-ramps for experienced professionals
nodes.definition: Experienced professionals (senior engineers, security specialists, policy veterans, operators) who want to move into AI safety have few structured on-ramps, and those already senior in adjacent fields lack the context, relationships and credibility to lead in this one; almost all fellowship infrastructure is built for students and early-career people.

nodes.name: Senior and specialist recruitment
nodes.definition: Safety organisations and frontier projects struggle to recruit senior or narrowly specialised people, such as security engineers with nation-state threat experience needed to reach RAND security levels SL4 and SL5, or policy veterans with legislative drafting experience, because ordinary recruiting channels and pay do not reach or persuade them.

nodes.name: Talent matchmaking
nodes.definition: With hundreds of organisations and a fragmented set of job boards, mailing lists and personal networks, a qualified person and a role that needs them frequently fail to find each other; Coefficient Giving names 'talent matchmaking' as a distinct gap even though 80,000 Hours, BlueDot and Kairos already do parts of this.

subareas.name: Evidence and forecasting
subareas.definition: The infrastructure that produces a reliable, shared, up-to-date picture of AI capabilities and real-world AI-caused harms, so that decisions elsewhere in the field rest on evidence rather than anecdote or a single company's account.

nodes.name: Capability forecasting
nodes.definition: Estimating how fast AI capabilities, compute use and algorithmic efficiency will grow, and when specific dangerous capabilities are likely to arrive, so that safety and policy work can be sequenced against a realistic timeline rather than guesswork.

nodes.name: Incident tracking
nodes.definition: A structured, ongoing record of AI-caused or AI-involved harms and near-misses (deployment failures, agent misbehaviour, misuse cases) that researchers, journalists and policymakers can query, analogous to aviation incident databases.

nodes.name: Incident investigation
nodes.definition: When an AI system behaves dangerously or unexpectedly in the wild, someone needs to do the equivalent of an air-accident investigation: reconstruct what happened, why, and what would have prevented it, independently of the company whose system was involved.

nodes.name: Living reviews of AI risk
nodes.definition: A canonical, regularly updated synthesis of the evidence on AI risks (capability, misuse, misalignment, structural) that a policymaker or new researcher can read to get an accurate, current picture, rather than reconstructing it from scattered papers, blog posts and lab claims.

nodes.name: Capability demonstrations for decision-makers
nodes.definition: Producing clear, credible, hands-on demonstrations of specific dangerous or surprising frontier model capabilities (autonomous cyber intrusion, self-exfiltration, deception) for an audience of policymakers and executives who otherwise only see capabilities through a company's own marketing or a dry benchmark score.

subareas.name: Watchdogs and accountability
subareas.definition: Independent organisations that scrutinise AI developers' safety claims and practices from outside, without needing the developer's cooperation, and support for insiders who speak out.

nodes.name: Lab accountability tracking
nodes.definition: Independent, recurring public ratings that compare frontier AI companies on safety practice, and ongoing tracking of changes to their published safety policies that flags when a promise is quietly weakened.

nodes.name: Whistleblower support
nodes.definition: Legal, financial and reputational support for employees of AI companies who want to raise safety concerns externally, separate from any internal reporting channel the company itself provides.

subareas.name: Communications and public engagement
subareas.definition: The journalism, polling, advocacy and explanatory work that shapes what the public, media and non-specialist decision-makers understand and believe about AI risk.

nodes.name: Public opinion research
nodes.definition: Systematic, methodologically rigorous polling of what the general public and specific constituencies think about AI risk and regulation, as opposed to occasional surveys run for a single campaign's messaging needs.

nodes.name: Explaining AI risk to the public
nodes.definition: Journalism and standing explanatory material (explainers, FAQs, accessible summaries) that accurately translate AI safety and governance research for people with no background, as opposed to material written for people already planning to enter the field.

nodes.name: Advocacy
nodes.definition: Organisations that campaign directly for public and political action on catastrophic AI risk, from grassroots protest movements to Washington-style legislative advocacy shops, distinct from research organisations that merely publish findings.

nodes.name: Field narrative strategy
nodes.definition: Deliberate, coordinated thinking about how AI risk is portrayed across mainstream media and culture over time (as opposed to sensationalised doom or dismissive hype), and how the field's various communicators avoid working at cross purposes.

subareas.name: Convenings and coordination
subareas.definition: The events, venues and dialogue infrastructure that let people working on AI safety, security and governance across organisations, sectors and countries find each other, build trust and coordinate.

nodes.name: Cross-sector convenings
nodes.definition: High-bandwidth in-person events that bring together the different groups shaping frontier AI (lab staff, national security officials, academics, journalists, civil society) who would not otherwise interact, to build shared understanding and personal trust across sector lines.

nodes.name: Subfield forums
nodes.definition: Focused events for a specific technical or policy subfield (control, security, interpretability) that bring together the smaller number of people working on that exact problem, distinct from broad cross-sector convenings aimed at general relationship-building.

nodes.name: Event infrastructure
nodes.definition: Shared logistical, venue and operational infrastructure that lets any AI safety organisation run a workshop, retreat or conference without rebuilding event-running capacity from scratch each time.

nodes.name: Regional community hubs
nodes.definition: Physical or organisational hubs (shared offices, local meetup networks, national chapters) that let AI safety researchers and newcomers in a given city or country find each other and collaborate, as opposed to the field being concentrated in Berkeley, London and a few other hub cities.

subareas.name: Research tooling and public goods
subareas.definition: Shared, non-rival resources (compute, datasets and environments, AI assistance, on-demand expertise) that lower the cost of doing safety and governance research for anyone in the ecosystem rather than any single organisation.

nodes.name: Compute for safety research
nodes.definition: Shared compute infrastructure (GPU clusters, cloud credits) available to the nonprofit and academic AI safety ecosystem, so that empirical safety research is not bottlenecked by researchers' individual ability to buy or beg for compute.

nodes.name: Safety datasets and environments
nodes.definition: Publicly available datasets, benchmarks and training/testing environments purpose-built to differentially advance safety research (rather than raw capability), which any researcher can use instead of building their own from scratch each time.

nodes.name: AI uplift for safety research
nodes.definition: Deliberately applying current frontier AI capabilities (coding assistance, literature synthesis, experiment automation) to speed up AI safety research itself, so that the safety ecosystem benefits from capability progress rather than being structurally slower than capabilities work that has no qualms about heavy AI-assisted development.

nodes.name: On-demand expertise for safety teams
nodes.definition: A shared pool of specialist expertise (legal, technical, security, policy) that frontier lab safety and governance teams, or smaller independent organisations, can call on for a specific question, rather than each team needing that expertise permanently in-house.

subareas.name: Strategy and prioritisation
subareas.definition: Research about how to think about AI risk and the field working on it at the highest level: what could go wrong and how, which scenarios are plausible, and which interventions and organisations should be prioritised given scarce money and talent.

nodes.name: Threat modelling
nodes.definition: Systematically developing, comparing and curating explicit models of how catastrophic outcomes from AI could actually occur (which actors, which failure chains, which warning signs), as a discipline in its own right rather than an implicit assumption buried inside individual papers and proposals.

nodes.name: Macrostrategy and scenarios
nodes.definition: Research that builds detailed, integrated narrative or quantitative scenarios of how transformative AI development could unfold over years, used to stress-test strategy rather than to produce a single point forecast.

nodes.name: Prioritisation and field strategy
nodes.definition: Research comparing the likely impact of different interventions within AI safety and governance, and studying the field itself as an ecosystem (which sub-problems are neglected, how organisations divide labour, how growth should be sequenced), to guide funders' and workers' decisions.

lens_definitions.name: Loss of control
lens_definitions.definition: Problems that matter most if AI systems come to act against their developers' intentions at scale.

lens_definitions.name: Agents
lens_definitions.definition: Problems that change when AI systems act on their own over long tasks, with tools and money.

lens_definitions.name: Democracy
lens_definitions.definition: Problems that bear on elections, public debate and how power is held to account.

lens_definitions.name: Defensive technology
lens_definitions.definition: Problems where building defensive tools is the main way to make progress.

lens_definitions.name: Open source
lens_definitions.definition: Problems shaped by openly released model weights.

lens_definitions.name: Critical infrastructure
lens_definitions.definition: Problems involving energy, water, telecoms, finance and other systems societies depend on.
